posts.title: Metallic silhouette for beginners
posts.description: Beginner’s guide to metallic silhouette at KRGC: chickens, pigs, turkeys, rams, distances, classes, and how to start without fancy gear.
posts.lede: Silhouette is simple to explain and hard to finish clean: knock the steel down or it does not count. Here is how the KRGC match is shaped for newer shooters.

posts.title: Come-up cards explained (and how to make one)
posts.description: What a come-up card is, why KRGC shooters carry one, and how to build a printable dope card with the club’s offline ballistics tool.
posts.lede: A come-up card is a cheat sheet for elevation (and sometimes wind) at known distances. It turns “I think hold a little high” into a number you already trusted at the bench.

posts.title: Eye and ear protection for outdoor ranges
posts.description: How to choose eye and ear protection for the Ketchikan Rod & Gun Club: glasses standards, muffs vs plugs, spectators, and wet-weather practicality.
posts.lede: Hearing damage is cumulative and permanent. Eye hits are instant. Both are optional injuries — dress for the line every time, including when you are “just watching.”

posts.title: How to shoot well in Ketchikan rain
posts.description: Keep groups honest in Southeast weather: lens care, footing, ammo storage, clothing, and match habits that work at the Ketchikan Rod & Gun Club.
posts.lede: If you only practice on bluebird days, you will only shoot well on bluebird days. KRGC is an outdoor club in a rainforest — rain is a skill, not a cancellation notice.

posts.title: Range commands and cease fire, explained
posts.description: Plain-language guide to KRGC range commands: cease fire, the line is hot, actions open, and what to do when someone is downrange.
posts.lede: Range talk is short on purpose. Learn the phrases before your first visit so you are not decoding them with a loaded rifle in your hands.

posts.title: Your first rimfire match: what to expect at KRGC
posts.description: What happens at the Ketchikan Rod & Gun Club monthly rimfire match — gear list, stages, loaner rifles, scoring, and how new shooters fit in.
posts.lede: The rimfire match is the easiest door into competition at KRGC. Show up with a .22, or empty-handed on loaner days, and you will leave knowing more than you did at 10:00.

posts.title: How to call wind on a Southeast Alaska range
posts.description: Practical wind reading for the Ketchikan Rod & Gun Club: flags, mirage, terrain funnels, and simple holds for rimfire and centerfire.
posts.lede: On Tongass, the wind rarely reads like a prairie range. It swirls off the timber, dies in the cut, and comes back from a new direction. Learn to watch the range — not just the flag at the bench.

posts.title: How to zero a .22 LR rifle for the rimfire match
posts.description: A clear 50-yard zero process for .22 LR at the Ketchikan Rod & Gun Club: rest, group, adjust, and confirm before match day.
posts.lede: A solid 50-yard zero is the difference between chasing clicks and stacking steel. Here is the process we walk new shooters through on the KRGC rimfire line.
